To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the entrepreneurial self-efficiency of innovators is significantly higher in comparison with the self-efficacy of graduate students of business.
innovators are more likely to start a new venture and that they are more confident in their entrepreneurial self-efficacies.
innovators and graduate business students differ significantly in entrepreneurial intentions, self-efficacy and the way they perceive their environment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of entrepreneurial self-efficiency in the prediction of nascent entrepreneurs in two transition economies.
two main questions: 1.
the role of the entrepreneurial self efficacy in the entrepreneurial process and its role as a predictor of nascent entrepreneurship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

entrepreneurial self-efficacies in the sample of Slovenian and Czech graduate students in business and innovators are similar to entrepreneurial self-efficies of graduate students in the United States, as reported by Chen et al. (1998).
the entrepreneurial self-efficiency of the two groups is not significantly different, but the innovator group is more likely to start a new venture than the graduate student group.
entrepreneurial self-efficacies are a good predictor for the entrepreneurial intentions of nascent entrepreneurs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the self-efficacy of the two groups of nascent entrepreneur in Slovenia and the Czech republic is not different from that of their Anglo-Saxon counterparts, but there are some differences between the two groups of the nascent entrepreneurs.
the self-efficacy scale developed in the Anglo-Saxon environment has a reasonable fit in the transition economy of Slovenia.
entrepreneurial self-efficacies are not significantly different between the two groups of nascent entrerpreneurs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the entrepreneurial self-efficiency construct can be successfully used in the transition economies.
there are some differences in entrepreneurial self-efficacies between innovators and graduate student entrepreneurs, which are related to their different backgrounds.
the self-efficacy of nascent entrepreneurs is not a stable construct, but it varies across groups.
